turns.prompt_text: A common critique of creative types and polymaths is that they start things and never finish them. They have all sorts of projects. They've just begun but will never finish come back to. It's like they just enjoy the excitement phase To be fair, following a project through to his conclusion is not always the correct answer but always jumping from project to project and starting new things is also wasteful
turns.response_html:
You’ve hit on the defining tension of the polymath. The criticism is absolutely valid, but the behavior isn't just a lack of discipline—it's a byproduct of how highly curious people process information and acquire skills.

The Mechanics of the "Excitement Phase"

What critics call the "excitement phase" is actually the period of rapid skill acquisition. When you apply deliberate practice to a brand new domain, the learning curve is practically vertical. You are absorbing new paradigms, breaking down complex rhythms, and solving structural problems.

But once you solve the core puzzle—once you prove to yourself that you can do it—the cognitive reward drops off a cliff. The remaining 80% of the project isn't discovery; it's just administrative execution and polishing. For a creative mind, executing a solved problem feels like tedious labor, which is why the urge to jump to the next unknown is so strong.

The Cost of the Infinite Pivot

You are right that blindly following a project to the bitter end isn't always correct. Forcing yourself to finish a prototype that has already served its educational purpose is a sunk-cost fallacy.

However, constantly jumping ship is highly wasteful. If you never push through the execution phase, you end up with a graveyard of half-finished frameworks and disconnected parts. You learn how to start a hundred things, but you never develop the specific resilience required to ship a complete, durable system.

How to Balance the Two

The goal isn't to force completion on everything, but to ensure that even your abandoned projects leave you with something valuable.

  • Define the "Done" State Upfront: Before starting, explicitly categorize the project. Is this a learning prototype or a production build? If it’s a prototype to test a specific mechanic, "done" means the mechanic is proven. You can walk away guilt-free.
  • Build Modularly: Architect your projects so they yield standalone, functional components early on. If you are building a complex system and lose interest halfway through, a modular approach ensures you at least walk away with a reusable tool or script, rather than a monolithic mess that only works if 100% finished.
  • Maintain a Lean Inventory of Active Projects: Treat your mental bandwidth the same way you would physical workspace. Keep a strictly lean inventory of active projects—perhaps one for deep focus and one for mechanical tinkering. If a shiny new idea appears, it doesn't get started until an active slot is cleared by either shipping or officially sunsetting a current project.

It comes down to intellectual honesty. Quitting is fine if it’s a strategic decision because the return on investment has diminished. It’s only a problem when quitting is just a reflex to avoid the friction of finishing.

They just become sold naturally
turns.response_html:
The garden metaphor is a perfect way to conceptualize this. It naturally separates the plant (the specific project or implementation) from the plot of land (the core problem or need). If a plant rots, the plot is still there, waiting for a new seed when the season is right. Sometimes, the environment changes and that plot gets shaded out naturally, meaning the problem solved itself without your intervention.

To audit your projects using this philosophy, you need a system that decouples the solution from the root problem. Here is a framework to structure that audit:

1. Decouple the Project from the Problem (Graphing the Plot)

Treat your active and inactive projects as nodes in a linked topology, distinctly separated from the "problem" nodes they are meant to solve.

  • List the Projects: Write down everything currently occupying mental or physical space.
  • Identify the Root Node: For each project, define the exact problem it exists to solve.
  • Assess the Link: Is the current project actually addressing the root problem, or has it mutated into an exercise in over-engineering?

2. The Problem-State Audit (Testing the Soil)

Before deciding what to do with a stale project, evaluate the underlying problem node itself.

  • The Naturally Solved: Has the ecosystem shifted? (e.g., A workflow you were trying to automate is no longer part of your routine). If the problem is dead, the project is dead. Archive it entirely.
  • The Persistent Need: The problem is still highly relevant, but the current project has stalled or rotted.
  • The Unnecessary: The problem still exists, but solving it yields no real value. It was a phantom need.

3. Pruning for a Lean Inventory

Just as you might maintain a strictly lean inventory of physical tools—keeping only what you use for immediate and frequent tasks—apply the same constraint to your active projects.

  • Limit Active Plots: You can only water so many things at once. Select a strictly limited number of projects to be in your "active" tier.
  • Move to the Seed Bank: If a project solves a persistent need but isn't a priority for your immediate routine, demote it. It is no longer an active project; it is a documented requirement waiting for future bandwidth.

4. Composting the Rot (Modular Extraction)

When a project has gone stale, but the underlying problem remains, do not just abandon the code or the hardware in a tangled mess.

  • Extract the Yield: Pull out the functional, modular components. Did you write a useful routing function? Did you figure out a specific mechanical tolerance?
  • Store the Fertilizer: Document those specific components and store them locally. When you eventually return to this "plot" to build a new solution, you won't be starting from scratch—you will have highly enriched soil to build upon.

By separating the need from the execution, you remove the guilt of a "failed" project. It didn't fail; it just wasn't the right crop for that season.
